EL3 Support: Introduction to Logarithms

Watch a Video to Learn

A narrated walkthrough of how to convert between exponential and logarithmic form and how to evaluate logarithms, including common and natural logarithms.

The video walkthrough is coming soon. In the meantime, the Quick Summary and the Try It tabs cover the same ideas.

Quick Summary

Every EL3 question comes back to one idea: a logarithm is an exponent. The value of \( \log_b x \) is the power you raise \( b \) to in order to get \( x \).

How the two forms match, and the slip to avoid
What you needHow to do itCommon slip
Exponential to logarithmic form\( b^y=x \) becomes \( \log_b x=y \). The base stays the base, the exponent becomes the value of the log, and the result goes inside.Swapping the base and the exponent, or putting the exponent inside the log.
Logarithmic to exponential form\( \log_b x=y \) becomes \( b^y=x \). Start at the base, raise it to the value of the log, and you land on the number inside.Putting the value of the log where the number inside belongs.
Evaluate a logarithmAsk: what power of the base gives the number inside? Rewrite the number inside as a power of the base.Answering with the number inside, or missing that \( \tfrac{1}{9}=3^{-2} \) and \( 4=16^{1/2} \) call for negative and fractional exponents.
Common and natural logarithms\( \log x \) with no base written means base 10. \( \ln x \) means base \( e \). Both follow the same rule as every other logarithm.Treating \( \ln \) as a different kind of operation, or thinking that \( \log \) has no base.

Your CheckIt problem will have different numbers than the examples here. The reasoning is what transfers.

Try It: Convert Between Forms

Make your best guess on each one, then check it. Ask yourself: which number is the base, which is the exponent, and which is the result?

Convert 1

\[ 3^4=81 \]

Which equation is the logarithmic form of this exponential equation?

The base of the exponential, 3, becomes the base of the log. The exponent, 4, becomes the value of the log, and 81 goes inside. Read it back as a check: \( \log_3 81=4 \) says "3 to the 4th power is 81." The logarithmic form is \( \log_3 81=4 \).

Convert 2

\[ 7^n=p \]

Which equation is the logarithmic form of this exponential equation?

Letters follow the same pattern as numbers. The base, 7, stays the base. The exponent, \( n \), is the value of the log. The result, \( p \), goes inside the log. Read it back: \( \log_7 p=n \) says "7 to the \( n \) is \( p \)." The logarithmic form is \( \log_7 p=n \).

Convert 3

\[ \log_5 125=3 \]

Which equation is the exponential form of this logarithmic equation?

The base of the log, 5, is the base of the power. The value of the log, 3, is the exponent. The number inside, 125, is the result. Check it: \( 5\cdot 5\cdot 5=125 \). The exponential form is \( 5^3=125 \).

Convert 4

\[ \log_b a=c \]

Which equation is the exponential form of this logarithmic equation?

Start at the base, \( b \). The value of the log, \( c \), is the exponent. The number inside, \( a \), is the result. Read it back: \( b^c=a \) says "\( b \) to the \( c \) is \( a \)." The exponential form is \( b^c=a \).

Try It: Evaluate

Rewrite the number inside as a power of the base, or ask: what power of the base gives this number?

Evaluate 1

\[ \log_2 32 \]

What is the value of this logarithm?

Ask: 2 to what power gives 32? Count the factors: \( 2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2\cdot 2=32 \), so \( 2^5=32 \). The value of the logarithm is that exponent. \( \log_2 32=5 \).

Evaluate 2

\[ \log_3\left(\tfrac{1}{9}\right) \]

What is the value of this logarithm?

Ask: 3 to what power gives \( \tfrac{1}{9} \)? Since \( 3^2=9 \), a negative exponent flips it to \( 3^{-2}=\tfrac{1}{9} \). A logarithm can be negative when the number inside is between 0 and 1. \( \log_3\left(\tfrac{1}{9}\right)=-2 \).

Evaluate 3

\[ \log_{16} 4 \]

What is the value of this logarithm?

Ask: 16 to what power gives 4? A square root undoes a square, so \( 16^{1/2}=\sqrt{16}=4 \), and the power is \( \tfrac{1}{2} \). Do not flip the base and the number: \( \log_4 16 \) would be 2, but here the base is 16. \( \log_{16}4=\tfrac{1}{2} \).

Try It: Common & Natural Logs

A log with no base written is a common logarithm, which means base 10. The natural logarithm, written \( \ln \), means base \( e \), where \( e\approx 2.718 \).

Common Log

\[ \log 0.01 \]

What is the value of this logarithm?

With no base written, the base is 10. Ask: 10 to what power gives 0.01? Since \( 0.01=\tfrac{1}{100}=\tfrac{1}{10^2}=10^{-2} \), the power is \(-2\). \( \log 0.01=-2 \).

Natural Log 1

\[ \ln 7=x \]

Which equation is the exponential form of this logarithmic equation?

\( \ln \) is a logarithm with base \( e \), so \( \ln 7=x \) means \( \log_e 7=x \). The base is \( e \), the exponent is \( x \), and the result is 7. The exponential form is \( e^x=7 \).

Natural Log 2

\[ \ln\left(e^5\right) \]

What is the value of this logarithm?

Ask: \( e \) to what power gives \( e^5 \)? The power is 5. The natural log undoes a power of \( e \). \( \ln\left(e^5\right)=5 \).
